lead: A plain PCFG gives a rule such as NP → NP PP one probability, whatever the words are. So it cannot weigh the triple (saw, man, with) against (ate, pizza, with): the words do not enter the rule probability. Words inside the PP such as 'telescope' are not heads under these head rules. A lexicalized PCFG writes each nonterminal with its head word and head tag, and conditions each rule on those heads. This makes the grammar sensitive to lexical choice. Shift-reduce parsing then builds the tree left to right with a stack of subtrees and a queue of input words; a classifier picks SHIFT or a REDUCE action. Parsers of this family are used in constituency and dependency analysis, and their features feed information extraction.
prereq: You need 3.5 for PCFG probabilities, 3.4 for PP attachment, and 3.3 for the CYK contrast.

blocks.text: Take 'she saw the man with the telescope' and 'she ate the pizza with a fork'. Each string has two trees. The PP 'with the telescope' may attach inside the NP (the man owns a telescope) or inside the VP (she used a telescope). A plain PCFG gives NP → NP PP and VP → VP PP fixed probabilities. The words 'saw', 'man' and 'with' do not change those numbers, so the grammar cannot use the lexical evidence that decides the case.

Lexicalization adds the head word to each nonterminal. The head is the word that carries the phrase's main meaning and fixes its category. Write a nonterminal as X(w, t): X is the phrase category, w is the head word, t is its part-of-speech tag. For example NP(man, N) is a noun phrase headed by 'man'.

A preterminal such as Det or N has no head child; its head is its word. Phrase rules percolate: S and VP take the verb, NP takes the noun, PP takes the preposition. Apply these rules recursively to annotate treebank trees. A lexicalized rule is A(a) → B(b) C(c), and its probability is conditioned on the three heads.
P(A(a) → B(b) C(c)) = P(A → B C | a, b, c)
blocks.where: A, B, C are phrase categories; a, b, c are their head words. The parent head a and both child heads b and c are the condition. A unary rule uses P(A → B | a, b).

blocks.text: Shift-reduce parsing reads the sentence once, left to right. It keeps a stack of subtrees already built and a queue of words not yet read. A classifier looks at the top of the stack, the next word, and their tags, then picks one action.

items: SHIFT: move the next word from the queue to the stack as a tagged preterminal subtree.
REDUCE-UNARY: pop one subtree and push a unary parent, such as NP → N.
REDUCE-BINARY-LEFT: pop the top two subtrees and push a parent whose head comes from the left child.
REDUCE-BINARY-RIGHT: same, but the head comes from the right child.
FINISH: stop when the queue is empty and the stack holds one tree.

blocks.text: Greedy search means one path only. A wrong early action changes the stack, and later actions build on that error, so one mistake can spoil the whole tree. Good features reduce this risk but do not remove it.

blocks.where: n is the number of words; u is the number of unary reductions. FINISH adds one more action, so total actions = 2n + u.

blocks.text: CYK (3.3), by contrast, fills a table for every span and keeps all parses. It is exhaustive and slower, but it cannot be misled by an early choice. Shift-reduce is fast and linear in the number of actions, but it commits early.

Lexicalized probabilities are sparse. A head word may appear in only a few treebank rules. Back off from the head word to the head tag to no lexical condition, and smooth the estimates. Without backoff, many lexicalized rules would have zero counts.

Collins-style parsers are one family of lexicalized statistical parsers. They annotate trees with heads, estimate lexicalized rule probabilities with smoothing, and search for the best tree. Shift-reduce parsers are another family: they replace exhaustive search with a learned action classifier. A neural shift-reduce dependency parser uses the same stack-and-queue control and learns features with a network; full neural architectures belong to Unit 6.

Use lexicalized PCFGs when word choice decides structure: PP attachment, coordination, subject-object choices. Use shift-reduce when speed matters and a labelled treebank is available. For long sentences, greedy errors are the main risk.

figure.caption: Ten boxes, one per action of the worked example; the small text is the stack after that action, with the last item on top. The highlighted reduce takes its head from the left child V(ate) and leaves S(ate) on the stack, ready for FINISH: 5 shifts + 4 reductions + 1 finish = 10 actions.

spec.title: Shift-reduce: the boy ate the cake
spec.aria: A ten-step flowchart of the shift-reduce actions for 'the boy ate the cake', each step showing the stack after it, from Det(the) at step 1 to S(ate) at steps 9 and 10, with the left-headed VP reduction highlighted.

examples.question: (a) Use S → NP VP, NP → Det N, VP → V NP, Det → the, N → boy | cake, V → ate. Shifted words are tagged preterminals: 'the' is Det and 'boy'/'cake' are N. Give the shift-reduce action sequence for 'the boy ate the cake'. Count SHIFT/REDUCE moves and total actions including FINISH. (b) In 'she saw the man with the telescope', the parses differ only in one rule. VP → VP PP with head 'saw' has p = 0.25; NP → NP PP with head 'man' has p = 0.05. Which attachment wins, and what is the ratio? Assume all other rules are shared.
steps: 1. Queue = [the, boy, ate, the, cake]; stack = [].
4. REDUCE-BINARY-RIGHT as NP → Det N, giving NP(boy); the noun boy is the head.
8. REDUCE-BINARY-RIGHT as NP → Det N, giving NP(cake); the noun cake is the head.
9. REDUCE-BINARY-LEFT as VP → V NP, head ate from the left child V; the stack becomes [NP(boy), VP(ate)].
10. REDUCE-BINARY-RIGHT as S → NP VP, head ate from the right child VP; the stack becomes [S(ate)].
11. FINISH. Count: 5 SHIFTs + 4 binary reductions = 9 building moves; FINISH adds 1, total 10.
12. Compare b: 0.25 vs 0.05. Ratio = 0.25 / 0.05 = 5.0. The VP rule is larger.
examples.answer: The PP attaches to the VP: 0.25 > 0.05, ratio 5.0, so the telescope is the instrument. The action sequence uses 9 building moves (5 SHIFTs, 4 binary reductions), plus FINISH, for 10 actions total.

traps: Conditioning a rule only on the parent head word. The child head words carry the lexical evidence; condition on all three heads as in P(A(a) → B(b) C(c)) = P(A → B C | a, b, c).
Treating a greedy shift-reduce choice as reversible. There is no backtracking; an early wrong reduce corrupts the stack and every later action.
Skipping backoff and smoothing. Lexicalized rules are sparse; use head word → head tag → no lexical condition, and smooth counts.

Reading LEFT/RIGHT as the direction of attachment. The label names the child that supplies the parent head: LEFT means the left of the two popped subtrees is the head, not that the phrase attaches to the left.
Miscounting actions. For n words with u unary reductions, building moves are 2n − 1 + u, and FINISH adds one, so total is 2n + u.

quiz.q: What two extra pieces of information does a lexicalized nonterminal X(w,t) carry beyond the category X?
quiz.a: The head word w and its part-of-speech tag t.

quiz.q: Why can a plain PCFG not choose the PP attachment in 'she saw the man with the telescope'?
quiz.a: The competing rules NP → NP PP and VP → VP PP have fixed probabilities. The words saw, man and with do not change the fixed rule probabilities, so lexical evidence is ignored.

quiz.q: For 'the dog saw the cat' with the same grammar and tagged preterminals, list the first four actions.
quiz.a: SHIFT the; SHIFT dog; REDUCE-BINARY-RIGHT as NP (head dog); SHIFT saw.

quiz.q: A shift-reduce parser makes a wrong binary reduce at word 4 of a 20-word sentence. Why can it not recover?
quiz.a: It is greedy and never backtracks. The wrong subtree stays on the stack, and later actions use it, so the error propagates to the root.

quiz.q: For an 8-word sentence with no unary reductions, how many building moves and total actions including FINISH?
Why does a lexicalized PCFG need backoff from head word to head tag?
quiz.a: Word-specific rule counts are sparse. A head word may be unseen with a rule, giving zero. Tag-level estimates are denser and can be smoothed.

quiz.q: Contrast CYK and shift-reduce on early errors.
quiz.a: CYK keeps all parses for every span, so no early commitment; an early choice cannot spoil it. Shift-reduce follows one path, so an early error propagates, but it is much faster.

beyond: Not for the exam. Transition-based parsers with neural classifiers are standard in dependency parsing and appear in fast constituency parsers. They keep the same stack-and-queue control but learn features from word embeddings. Search for 'transition-based parsing', 'arc-standard', and 'lexicalized PCFG Collins'. Modern span-based neural parsers often replace greedy transition parsing, but the greedy idea remains a strong speed baseline.
